title: Haystack: one disk read per photo
dek: In 2010 the largest social network explained why storing 260 billion photos as files was slow: the file system's own bookkeeping cost more disk reads than the photos. Its fix packs millions of photos into huge files and keeps a tiny index in memory, so each photo costs one disk read.

items: Stored one file per photo, every read paid extra disk operations just to find the file, because file-system metadata for billions of files doesn't fit in memory.
Haystack appends photos as 'needles' into 100 GB volume files, each kept on three machines, and keeps a small in-memory index of where each photo starts.
So a photo costs one disk read. Deletes only set a flag; compaction later rewrites volumes without the deleted photos.

body.x: The paper: "Finding a needle in Haystack: Facebook's photo storage" by Doug Beaver, Sanjeev Kumar, Harry C. Li, Jason Sobel and Peter Vajgel, OSDI 2010.

When the paper was written the site stored over 260 billion images, about 20 PB, and received a billion new photos, about 60 TB, every week, and served over a million images a second at peak. A CDN served the popular photos well, but photo traffic has a long tail: old photos are requested rarely, yet together they make up a large share of requests, and those requests miss the CDN and reach storage.

Storage was network-attached file servers, one file per photo. Reading a file means finding its directory entry, then its inode, then the data, and with billions of files that metadata didn't fit in memory. Early on a photo took around ten disk operations; smaller directories brought it to about three. The disks were spending most of their time on bookkeeping.

body.cap: The photo bytes are the same in both designs. What changes is where the 'where is it' lives: on disk, spread over directory entries and inodes, or in a compact index in memory that turns a photo ID straight into a disk offset.

items: Store machines hold physical volumes, each a single file of about 100 GB containing millions of photos. Each logical volume is copied onto three physical volumes on different machines.
Each photo, a needle, sits in the volume with a header (its ID, flags, size) and a checksum. Every photo is kept in four sizes.
The store keeps an in-memory map from photo ID to offset and size, saved to an index file so a restarted machine doesn't have to scan 100 GB to rebuild it.
A directory service maps logical volumes to machines, picks which volume takes each upload, and builds photo URLs that say which CDN, cache and store machine to ask.
An internal cache in front of the stores holds recently uploaded photos, which get most of the requests the CDN misses.

body.cap: Writes are appends, so they are fast and simple. A delete only marks the needle, and space comes back during compaction, when live needles are copied to a fresh volume.

body.x: Each usable terabyte cost about 28% less than the file servers it replaced and served about four times as many reads per second. A later paper from the same company moved older, rarely viewed photos to cheaper storage that uses erasure coding instead of three full copies.

items: For the Photo sharing problem, say where each part lives: photo bytes in object storage or Haystack-style volumes, metadata in a database, popular photos in a CDN.
Name the small-file problem: billions of small objects stored as separate files waste disk reads on metadata. Pack them into large files and index them.
Mention the long tail: a CDN doesn't help with old photos, so the storage layer must serve them efficiently.
Writes as appends, deletes as flags, and compaction later: the same shape as log-structured storage everywhere.

body.x: Each upload is resized into four versions, from a thumbnail to a large view, and all four are stored. Resizing once at upload is cheaper than resizing on every view, and the small versions are what feeds and grids request most. It is a common trade: spend storage once to save work on every read.
